subject: Commercial terms: decoupled burn-rate fallback & overage mitigation
messages:
From: Elena Soto <elena.soto@medisys.com>
To: olga.petrov@redwood.ai, procurement@medisys.com
Date: Wed, 19 Aug 2026 09:13:00 -0700
Subject: RFP commercial clarifications — burn profile volatility and billing fallback

Hi Olga / Redwood team,

Thanks for the quick overview at yesterday's vendor briefing. Our procurement and finance teams reviewed the draft ratecard and have two commercial questions we need written responses for in the RFP:

1) Our workload pattern is spiky — sustained baseline plus unpredictable bursts triggered by nightly batch jobs and weekly analytics cycles. We need a concrete fallback that protects our monthly bill from an unexpected 3x burst for up to 48 hours while preserving predictable unit economics the rest of the month.

2) We prefer an approach that decouples committed spend from short-term burn so we can keep a predictable committed invoice while still being able to burst. Please outline a practical "burn-rate fallback" construct and how overages would be capped/credited during reconciliation.

Can you provide a short written proposal (max 2 pages) and an example invoice reconciliation for a sample month? We are on an aggressive procurement timeline — aim to get this in by Friday if possible.

Regards,
Elena Soto
Senior Procurement Manager
MediSys Health

From: olga.petrov@redwood.ai

Subject: Re: RFP commercial clarifications — burn profile volatility and billing fallback

Elena — thanks, and appreciate the clarity on procurement's constraints. High level answer below; I'll attach a brief worked example and the spreadsheet for your finance team.

Summary (TL;DR):
- Proposal: "Decoupled Burn Fallback" — customers sign a monthly committed token spend (invoice-guaranteed). We layer a temporary burst cushion (pre-provisioned burst credits) and a capped overage window. If burst usage exceeds cushion, overages get billed at a higher, pre-agreed surge rate but are subject to a monthly cap expressed as a percentage of the committed invoice. At reconciliation, any unused burst cushion credits can be rolled forward or credited back per the chosen cadence.

Key mechanics (short):
- Commit: monthly committed tokens (e.g., 1.2B tokens) at the negotiated unit rate.
- Burst cushion: a modest pre-funded cushion (e.g., 10–30% of commit depending on SLAs) available immediately; priced at committed rate and amortized into the invoice or pre-bought as credits.
- Surge rate & cap: additional tokens beyond cushion billed immediately at a surge rate (e.g., 2.5x base) but subject to a monthly overage cap (e.g., 35% of committed invoice value).
- Reconciliation: Monthly true-up that applies any pre-purchased cushion credit, then applies overage cap. If overage cap is hit, we trigger automatic routing to an agreed secondary model variant (lower-cost quantized variant) and provide invoice crediting for any excessive delta on request.

Attached: Redwood_Commercial_Sheet_Q3.xlsx (worked example with a 3x 48-hour burst scenario) and a draft MSA excerpt with cap language.

Internal note to Marissa / David: please review the surge-rate ladder and suggested cap percentages in the spreadsheet. I propose the initial commercial position below (Marissa: confirm discounting and David: confirm Ops feasibility for automatic model-fallback when the cap is hit).

Next steps: Elena — if this looks aligned we can convert the worked example into contract language and include a 60-day pilot with a reduced commit and the same smoothing rules.

Best,
Olga Petrov

Subject: Re: RFP commercial clarifications — burn profile volatility and billing fallback

Quick read — looks good. A few proposals to firm up numbers for the RFP: 

1) Cushion sizing: recommend default 20% of commit for customers with >10% month-over-month variance; 30% for extremely spikey (we should show both in the sheet).
2) Surge ladder: 1.0x for commit cushion (base), 2.0x for first overflow band, 2.5x beyond that. We should include a blended rate example so finance can see effective $/1k tokens if cap is hit.
3) Cap mechanics: prefer cap expressed as % of committed invoice (35%) rather than a token count — easier to reconcile and limits invoice unpredictability.

Ops point (David): is automatic fallback to a quantized variant feasible within a 15-minute window after cap breach? Need confirmation on model variant availability in Dedicated regions. If not, we should agree to a manual fallback and a 24-hour notification SLA.

I'll update the spreadsheet with the two cushion profiles, surge ladder, and blended-rate table.

-M

--
Marissa Cole
Head of Commercial Deals | Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwood.ai

From: olga.petrov@redwood.ai

Elena — attached is the two-page write-up and the worked example spreadsheet we discussed. Highlights: 

- Option A (Standard cushion): 20% cushion, surge ladder 2.0x / 2.5x, monthly overage cap = 35% of committed invoice.
- Option B (Aggressive cushion): 30% cushion with slightly lower surge multipliers and a pilot discount for the first 2 months.
- Pilot option: 60-day pilot at 50% commit with identical smoothing rules to prove variance assumptions.

Invoice example included: shows a model month with a 3x 48-hour burst that draws full cushion and triggers partial surge billing; reconciliation calculates net charged amount and shows how a cap is applied and how invoice credits would be computed.

Requested next steps: please confirm which option (A or B) you prefer and whether you would like the pilot. If agreed, we'll translate the cap & fallback language into a short contract exhibit and circulate with the draft MSA for your legal/procurement review.

Thanks — looking forward to moving this to a pilot.

Best regards,
Olga Petrov
Senior Account Executive | Redwood Inference
